highlights:
## No. 3: CoreWeave, the GPU Cloud Layer

CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) rents NVIDIA GPU clusters by the hour and by multi-year contract to AI labs, hyperscalers, and enterprises that either cannot get chips or do not want to operate them. Customers include Databricks, Grammarly, Isomorphic Labs, Hudson River Trading, and Runway ML, and CoreWeave was the first cloud to bring up NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72.

The numbers are eye-popping. Q2 2026 revenue hit $2.58 billion, up 112.3% year over year, with a revenue backlog around $104 billion and more than $25 billion in net new customer commitments added early in Q3. Active power expanded to 1.5 GW, with contracted power of roughly 3.7 GW. CEO Michael Intrator said “CoreWeave reached an important inflection point this quarter as our scale began to translate into expanding operating leverage.”

The bull case is scarcity: demand exceeds supply and July pricing was raised roughly 25% across SKUs. The risk is the balance sheet. CapEx ran $6.42 billion in the quarter, free cash flow was negative $5.74 billion, and debt/equity sits at 8.94. Interest expense alone was $640 million versus $267 million a year earlier. Shares closed at $94.94, down 5.27% over the past year despite the operational blowout. This is the highest-beta way to play AI infrastructure.

results.title: Europe's Sovereign GPU Price Table: The Two Break-Evens That Decide Rent-vs-Own Inference | bex.co
highlights:
An H100 in Germany costs $2.80 an hour. The same class of GPU in France costs $3.20. Neither vendor will sell you an H200 or a B200 at any price, neither offers spot, and neither can be compelled by a US court order to hand over your data. That is the entire European sovereign-GPU market in one paragraph — and if you run inference for EU users, that paragraph is also your shortlist.

...

## The table, up front​

All rates below are per-GPU, on-demand hourly, from published September 2026 numbers. Hyperscaler rows are EU-region contrast, not recommendations.

| Provider | Region | H100/hr | H200 | B200 | Spot | CLOUD Act exposure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hetzner Cloud | NBG, FSN (Germany) | ~$2.80 | Not available | Not available | No | No |
| OVHcloud | FR, DE, UK | ~$3.20 | Not available (Paris GA is managed-only) | Not available | No | No |
| Scaleway | FR (Paris) | ~$2.99 (H100 PCIe) | Limited | B300 available EU-first | Partial | No |
| AWS (EU region) | EU regions | ~$6.88 | ~$4.98 | ~$14.24 | Yes | Yes |
| Azure (EU region) | EU regions | ~$12.29 | ~$13.78 | TBA | Yes | Yes |

Three things to read off before the detail. First, the sovereign discount is real: Hetzner's H100 rate undercuts AWS's EU-region H100 by roughly 60%. The broader market tells the same story — median on-demand H100 pricing runs about $4.17/hr on dedicated GPU clouds versus about $7.89 on hyperscalers, an ~89% premium for the same silicon.

...

Currencies normalized to USD throughout so the comparison is checkable: Hetzner's dedicated GEX131 GPU server lists at €889/month, which Hetzner itself quotes as $989/month. A month is 730 hours. Stated once, used everywhere below.

The own-side candidate is the GEX131: a dedicated box with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (96 GB) at $989/month flat, no setup fee, IPv4 included — about $1.35/hr if you run it wall-to-wall. The rent-side candidates are the two hourly rows above. Full-month totals at 730 hours:

| Option | Monthly total at 730 hrs | Effective $/hr |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Own: GEX131 dedicated ($989 flat) | $989 | $1.35 |
| Rent: Hetzner Cloud H100 at $2.80/hr | $2,044 | $2.80 |
| Rent: OVHcloud H100 at $3.20/hr | $2,336 | $3.20 |

At full utilization, owning saves ~$1,055/month (52%) against Hetzner's own hourly rate and ~$1,347/month (58%) against OVHcloud. The break-evens — the utilization where flat beats metered — fall out by division:

- vs Hetzner hourly: $989 ÷ $2.80 ≈ 353 hours/month (~48% utilization). Past roughly 11–12 hours a day, own the box.
- vs OVHcloud hourly: $989 ÷ $3.20 ≈ 309 hours/month (~42% utilization). Past roughly 10 hours a day, own the box.

...

The most consequential cell in the table is "Not available." Neither Hetzner Cloud nor OVHcloud self-service rents H200 or B200 capacity as of September 2026; OVHcloud's H200 footprint (Paris GA, Milan) sits behind its managed AI products, not the public-cloud hourly meter. Market-wide, the generation ladder is steep — H200 on-demand averages ~$4.00/GPU-hr with a 25–30% premium over H100, B200 averages ~$6.11, and hyperscaler B200 rows reach $8.60–$14.24 — but none of that matters to a team that cannot clear compliance on a US-incorporated vendor, because the sovereign shelf stops at Hopper's first rung.

results.title: What is a neocloud, and how does it price GPUs?
highlights:
A neocloud rents Nvidia GPUs and nothing else; CoreWeave's HGX H100 node lists at $6.16 per GPU-hour on-demand, up to 60% cheaper on a multi-year commit.

...

A neocloud is a cloud provider, such as CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius or Crusoe, built entirely around renting Nvidia GPUs rather than general-purpose compute; it prices capacity on two tiers, a high hourly on-demand rate for flexibility and a discounted multi-year committed rate, with the gap (CoreWeave's HGX H100 runs $6.16 per GPU-hour on-demand versus up to 60% less reserved) funding the debt used to buy the GPUs in the first place.

...

- ▸ A neocloud is a cloud provider built entirely around GPU rental, a term SemiAnalysis coined on 3 October 2024 to separate CoreWeave-style specialists from AWS, Azure and GCP.
- ▸ CoreWeave's on-demand HGX H100 node lists at $49.24/hour for 8 GPUs, or $6.16 per GPU-hour, versus up to 60% off for a multi-year committed contract.
- ▸ The blended market rate for an H100 SXM was $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26 per Ornn Data's index, well under any single neocloud's posted on-demand sticker.
- ▸ CoreWeave's revenue backlog reached $99.4 billion as of 2026-03-31, the contracted demand that lets it borrow against unbuilt data centers to keep expanding.
- ▸ Neocloud spot pricing swings hard: CoreWeave's HGX H100 spot rate is $19.71/hour, 60% below on-demand, because unsold capacity is a sunk cost the moment the GPU is idle.

...

A neocloud is a cloud provider built entirely around renting Nvidia GPUs, nothing else, and it prices that capacity on two tiers: a high hourly rate for anyone who shows up without a commitment, and a discount of up to 60% for anyone willing to sign a multi-year contract. CoreWeave’s on-demand HGX H100 node runs $49.24 an hour for eight GPUs, or $6.16 per GPU-hour, a rate you can read straight off its public pricing page. The skill this post is really teaching is how to read that gap between on-demand and reserved pricing and understand why it exists, because it tells you exactly what a neocloud is betting on and what happens to your bill if that bet goes wrong.

...

A neocloud is a specialist cloud provider, CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius and Crusoe are the four SemiAnalysis classified as “neocloud giants” in its October 2024 taxonomy, that sells GPU rental almost exclusively instead of the broad service catalog a hyperscaler like AWS or Azure bundles. Pricing runs on two tracks: an on-demand hourly rate priced for flexibility and idle-capacity risk, and a reserved or committed rate discounted against multi-year contracts, up to 60% off on CoreWeave’s own pricing page. A blended market rate sits below either extreme: Ornn Data’s H100 SXM index settled at $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26, versus CoreWeave’s $6.16 on-demand sticker for the same chip. The reserved discount exists because a signed, multi-year contract is exactly what lets a neocloud borrow money to buy the GPUs in the first place, so the price you’re quoted is really a reflection of how much certainty you’re giving the provider.

...

A neocloud’s business starts with debt, not with a data center. The provider needs tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs, each one a five- or six-figure capital outlay before power and networking, and it typically can’t fund that from operating cash flow alone. So it signs a multi-year take-or-pay contract with a hyperscaler or an AI lab first, then uses that contract as collateral to borrow the money to buy the hardware. CoreWeave’s relationship with Microsoft is the clearest public example: the two companies have operated under a Master Service Agreement dating to February 2023, and that scale of committed demand is the kind of anchor a lender underwrites against. Once the GPUs are bought and racked inside a leased or purpose-built facility (What is a data center?), the neocloud has to sell every hour of capacity it can, because the GPUs depreciate and the debt service comes due whether or not anyone is renting that hour. Unlike a hyperscaler, which can shift idle GPU capacity onto dozens of other services (storage, databases, general compute), a neocloud has no such fallback: an unsold GPU-hour is just gone.

That single fact, an idle GPU costs money and an idle GPU earns nothing, explains the whole pricing structure. On-demand rates are set high because that customer is asking for maximum flexibility with zero commitment, so the provider prices in both the option value it’s giving up and the risk that the same hour goes unsold to someone else. Reserved or committed rates are set low because that customer is providing exactly what a lender wants to see: predictable, contracted cash flow over a multi-year term, the kind of backlog that let CoreWeave carry $99.4 billion in signed but not-yet-delivered revenue as of 2026-03-31. Spot pricing sits at the opposite extreme from on-demand: CoreWeave lists spot HGX H100 capacity at $19.71 an hour, 60% below its on-demand rate, because spot is explicitly the leftover capacity a provider would rather sell cheap than leave idle. The underlying Nvidia H100 silicon (What is a GPU?) doesn’t change between these tiers; only the certainty attached to the rental does.

## The numbers

The gap between on-demand and reserved pricing, and between one neocloud’s sticker price and the broader market, is the whole story. CoreWeave’s own pricing page lists three current Nvidia generations, each as an eight-GPU HGX node:

| GPU (8x HGX node) | On-demand, per node | On-demand, per GPU-hour | Spot, per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | $49.24/hr | $6.16 | $2.46 |
| H200 | $50.44/hr | $6.31 | $2.62 |
| B200 | $68.80/hr | $8.60 | $4.26 |

Lambda prices per GPU rather than per node: its H100 SXM runs $3.99 to $4.29 per GPU-hour on-demand and its B200 SXM6 runs $6.69 to $6.99, both lower than CoreWeave’s equivalent on-demand figures, which is consistent with Lambda competing on price within the same neocloud-giant tier. Against both of those sits Ornn Data’s blended H100 index, the same number that answers how much does it cost to rent an H100 per hour?, which settled at $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26, below every on-demand figure above because the index averages across many providers and contract structures, including the deep reserved discounts that never show up on a public on-demand rate card. CoreWeave doesn’t publish what those reserved rates actually are by term length or volume, only that committed usage saves “up to 60% over on-demand prices,” so the number a given customer pays sits somewhere between that index average and the on-demand ceiling depending entirely on what they’re willing to sign. Underneath all of this, CoreWeave reported $2.078 billion in Q1 2026 revenue and a 56% adjusted EBITDA margin against that $99.4 billion backlog, evidence that the reserved side of the business, not the on-demand sticker, is what actually funds the buildout.

...

Spot capacity is the third lever, and it’s the right call for anything genuinely interruptible: batch inference, checkpointed training, anything that can tolerate a GPU getting reclaimed mid-job in exchange for CoreWeave’s 60%-off spot rate.

results.title: Why H100 Rental Prices Rose 40% While Token Prices Fell
highlights:
> TL;DR: H100 rental prices rose almost 40% between October 2025 and March 2026, from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour on one-year contracts, while API token prices kept falling. The cost floor under inference is rising even as the sticker price above it drops, and every self-hosting business case written before that shift is now wrong.

...

The number worth reading is the rental contract. H100 one-year rental pricing rose from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, close to 40%, and on-demand capacity was described as sold out across all GPU types, with half the providers surveyed unable to quote even 8 nodes of H100s or H200s (SemiAnalysis's H100 rental price index). That is not a market pricing in abundance. That is a market rationing.

...

```
At the October 2025 rate:
  8 GPUs x $1.70/GPU-hour            = $13.60 / hour
  $13.60 x 8,760 hours               = $119,136 / year

At the March 2026 rate:
  8 GPUs x $2.35/GPU-hour            = $18.80 / hour
  $18.80 x 8,760 hours               = $164,688 / year

Delta: $45,552 / year, +38.2%, on identical hardware

...

In the CFO commentary accompanying its second-quarter fiscal 2027 results, filed 26 August 2026, Nvidia disclosed that its supply commitments increased from $119 billion in the prior quarter to $279 billion, "primarily related to the procurement of memory" (Nvidia's Q2 FY2027 CFO commentary, filed with the SEC). The company also said it had partnered with its supplier network "to secure the critical components needed to meet demand for the next several years."

Read that as an engineering statement and it is precise. A $160 billion increase in forward commitments, concentrated on memory, is a company locking down the input it expects to be scarce.

...

This is why the rental price behaves differently from the token price. A provider can cut a token rate tomorrow by deciding to earn less per token. Nobody can decide their way into more HBM. When the scarce input has a multi-year lead time and the demand for it is growing at the rate AI capex is growing, the clearing price of a GPU-hour goes up and stays up, regardless of what any rate card says. The same physical wall shows up inside serving too, which is why GPU utilization economics reward batching so heavily.

...

Because demand for inference capacity outran physical supply, and the constraint moved from chip fabrication to high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging. One-year H100 contracts rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026, and on-demand capacity was reported sold out across GPU types.

...

### Q: How much does an H100 cost to rent per hour?

Published index pricing for one-year H100 contracts was $2.35 per GPU-hour as of March 2026, up from a $1.70 low in October 2025. On-demand and short-term rates sit higher and vary widely by provider and region, and during the 2026 crunch several providers could not quote capacity at any advertised rate. Treat a quoted rate as valid only for the term you can actually sign.

results.title: GPU Marketplaces Are Cheapest, Until They Aren't | Blog
highlights:
The short version: marketplaces are strongest where supply is fragmented. Thousands of independent hosts can undercut dedicated clouds on consumer GPUs. New data center accelerators are different. The providers that own large, uniform fleets often set the price floor themselves.

...

Marketplace-style providers occupy seven of the cheapest ten positions for RTX 5090 and RTX 4090, four for H200 and A100 SXM, three for H100 SXM, and two for B200.

| GPU | Marketplaces in cheapest ten | Share | Providers with a listing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RTX 5090 | 7/10 | 70% | 14 |
| RTX 4090 | 7/10 | 70% | 18 |
| H200 | 4/10 | 40% | 39 |
| A100 SXM | 4/10 | 40% | 37 |
| H100 SXM | 3/10 | 30% | 48 |
| B200 | 2/10 | 20% | 28 |

...

> Price floor is not scalable price. A cheapest listing is one machine in one place. It does not tell you what ten, 64, or 256 identical GPUs will cost, or whether they are available at all.

This suggests three useful GPU price concepts:

- Price floor: the cheapest currently observed listing.
- Available price: the cheapest capacity you can provision now for the required configuration.
- Scale price: the cheapest price available for a meaningful cluster of identical GPUs with the networking and reliability the workload needs.

| Omega Gradient | Aggregator + broker | Sourced reserved clusters | Hourly, prepaid | No | No | None current |

...

Lium publishes individual nodes with city-level locations, reliability ratings, and separate per-GPU and per-node hourly prices. Its catalog covers consumer cards through B200 and B300, with secure and spot tiers.

It also exposes a common pricing trap. A cheap per-GPU rate may require renting a 4x or 8x node. The relevant number is the minimum bill, not just the normalized GPU-hour rate.

...

## How to read a marketplace price

Before treating a low number as comparable, ask what it is attached to.

- Per GPU or per node? A normalized rate can hide a 4x or 8x minimum rental. ComputePrices shows per-GPU rates, but the provider's checkout total is what matters.
- On-demand or interruptible? Vast interruptible bids, Runpod spot pods, Lium spot, Spheron spot, and Compute Cheap capacity can be reclaimed.
- Which tier? Community, secure, spot, standard, and dedicated tiers are different products. Compare them as such.
- Which machine? Check CPU, RAM, storage, bandwidth, location, and host reliability before assuming two GPUs are equivalent.
- Is it in stock? Some providers expose availability. Others publish catalog prices even when no capacity can be provisioned.
- Can it scale? Confirm the number of identical GPUs, topology, and cluster price before planning around the cheapest row.
- Who sets the price? An aggregator's rate is its own. It may sit above or below the underlying supplier's direct price.

...

results.title: AI Price Hikes 2026: The 10 Nobody Warned You About
highlights:
Both waves are broken out in the OVHcloud post, and the general mechanism in why your VPS price is going up.

## 2. Graphics cards absorbed three kit hikes in seven months

Nvidia passed memory costs to board partners three times in 2026. TrendForce reported January at 10 to 15 percent, with 16GB-and-above models at 15 to 20 percent. May was narrow and hit the RTX 5090 line only. Late July was the broad one at 20 to 30 percent, reaching every GeForce RTX model.

Those compound. A mid-range card that missed the May increase is roughly 32 to 50 percent more expensive than in January, before a retailer adds anything. An Asus TUF RTX 5080 went from $1,199 to $1,595, or 33 percent, which sits at the bottom of that band. The unabsorbed remainder is the risk to anyone waiting. Full chain in GPU prices in 2026, with current levels on the GPU price tracker.
